content: Studies have shown that adherence to interventions is higher when the product is provided intermittently. This is likely because such a regimen reduces the pressure and anxiety experienced by caregivers. For further details on adherence, refer to the section titled Dissemination and Implementation. The first systematic review included 18 trials, with 21 references listing the published articles. According to the WHO guideline, the use of multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by infants and young children aged 6–23 months, as well as children aged 2–12 years, is an effective intervention to reduce anemia and iron deficiency. This intervention has been shown to be equally effective in areas with varying prevalence rates of anemia and malaria, including regions with sporadic malaria cases, and regardless of the intervention duration (ranging from 2 to 18 months). The systematic review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials, with either individual or cluster randomization. The target population was children aged 2–12 years at the start of the intervention, without specific health problems, although some participants were at risk of anemia or iron deficiency due to the high prevalence of these conditions in the study settings. The intervention involved the consumption of foods fortified at the point of use with MNPs containing at least iron, in any dose, frequency, or duration. Comparisons were made with no intervention, placebo, iron-only supplements, iron and folic acid supplements, or the same multiple micronutrients provided as supplements. The trials assessed outcomes such as anemia prevalence (hemoglobin <110 g/L for children under 5 years and <115 g/L for children aged 5–11 years, adjusted for altitude), hemoglobin levels (g/L), iron deficiency (ferritin concentrations <15 μg/L), ferritin levels (μg/L), all-cause mortality (number of deaths during the trial), and diarrhea (defined as three or more liquid stools per day). Subgroup analyses included malaria status. A total of 12 trials with 5,720 participants from lowand middle-income countries in Asia, Africa, and the Americas were included. Five trials involved children under 5 years, four included only children aged 5 years or older, and three included children both younger and older than 5 years. The interventions lasted between 2 and 12 months, and the MNP formulations contained between 2 and 18 micronutrients. The settings included schools, feeding centers, and communities. Most trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias. The second systematic review included 12 trials with 16 references listing the published articles. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology, and the summary of findings is available in Annex 2C. No trials reported on three other comparisons. Acceptability was not consistently considered in the trials and could not be assessed in this review. The WHO guideline strongly recommends point-of-use fortification of complementary foods with iron-containing MNPs for infants and young children aged 6–23 months in populations where anemia is a public health problem. This intervention improves iron status and reduces anemia, supported by moderate-quality evidence. A suggested scheme for point-of-use fortification includes 12.5 mg of ferrous sulfate heptahydrate or equivalent amounts in other iron compounds. Sodium iron EDTA (NaFeEDTA) is generally not recommended for children aged 6–12 months due to its higher bioavailability, and the appropriate dose range requires further research. For children aged 2–12 years, point-of-use fortification with iron-containing MNPs is also recommended in populations where anemia is a public health problem. This intervention improves iron status and reduces anemia, supported by moderate-quality evidence. The recommended dose is 2.5 mg of ferrous sulfate heptahydrate or equivalent amounts in other iron compounds. If NaFeEDTA is used, the dose of elemental iron should be reduced by 3–6 mg due to its higher bioavailability. The formulation of MNPs can include or exclude other vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin A and zinc, to achieve 100% of the recommended nutrient intake (RNI), considering technical and sensory properties. The guideline development group emphasized the importance of considering likely consumption from other sources, including home diets and fortified foods, when establishing the composition of the sachets. Countries should have a national strategy for the prevention and control of micronutrient malnutrition, integrating point-of-use fortification with other interventions such as fortified foods, iron supplements, and lipid-based nutrient supplements. Programs should include behavior-change strategies to promote awareness, correct use of MNPs, proper preparation, and feeding practices, as well as training for healthcare workers on nutrition counseling and demonstrating the correct use of MNPs. In malaria-endemic areas, the provision of iron, including MNPs, should be implemented alongside measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria, such as insecticide-treated bed nets, vector-control programs, prompt diagnosis, and effective antimalarial therapy. If sugar or other foods are fortified with vitamin A, the inclusion of vitamin A in MNPs should be carefully assessed to avoid excessive intake. Research gaps identified by the WHO guideline development group include the need for further studies on the functional, developmental, and adverse outcomes of MNP use, particularly in settings with high rates of infectious diseases and poor access to healthcare. Research is also needed to determine the lowest effective dose of NaFeEDTA, the nutritional improvement of complementary foods, the optimal composition and dose of MNPs, and the risks and benefits of different frequencies of use. Additionally, formative research is required to guide the design of programs distributing MNPs and to identify the minimum behavior-change strategies needed to support their adoption and appropriate use. The guideline will be disseminated through electronic media, including slide presentations, the WHO Nutrition website, and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA), which compiles WHO guidelines and complementary documents such as systematic reviews.
